Summary

This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features. The authors argue that although recent CBM constructions can approach the accuracy of direct feature-based classifiers on the source domain, they can degrade substantially under distribution shift, sometimes more than non-interpretable baselines. To address this, the paper proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: (i) Concept Score Alignment (CSA), which adapts concept vectors to align target concept-score distributions to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics; (ii) Linear Probing Adaptation (LPA), which adapts the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-labels; and (iii) Residual Concept Bottleneck (RCB), which adds new residual concepts and a residual linear head to compensate for incomplete concept sets. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 suggest substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to direct zero-shot or linear-probe baselines.

Overall assessment

I think this is an interesting and timely paper. The problem setting is meaningful: if CBMs are to be useful in deployment, they should not only be interpretable on the source domain but also remain useful under shift. The paper’s central empirical observation—that CBMs are not automatically more robust than direct FM-based predictors—is important. The proposed decomposition into concept adaptation, classifier adaptation, and residual concept expansion is intuitive and reasonably well motivated. The empirical results are promising, especially on concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.

That said, I have several concerns about the paper’s technical clarity, evaluation methodology, and the strength of some claims around interpretability and robustness. In particular, the method relies heavily on pseudo-labels from non-interpretable predictors, the theoretical framing is more definitional than analytical, and some experimental choices make it difficult to isolate what is gained specifically from “concept-based adaptation” versus generic source-free adaptation of a shallow classifier. I view the paper as promising but not yet fully convincing in its current form.

Strengths

1. Important problem formulation
The paper addresses a real gap in the literature: test-time adaptation for interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines built on foundation models. This is a natural and practically relevant setting.

2. Clear motivation
The motivating observation is compelling: source-domain parity between CBMs and direct classifiers does not imply robustness under shift. Figure 1 and the broader framing make this point well.

3. Modular method design
The three components of CONDA are conceptually sensible:
- CSA targets instability in concept extraction under low-level shifts.
- LPA targets mismatch in concept-to-label mapping under concept-level shifts.
- RCB targets incompleteness of the concept bank.
This decomposition is one of the strongest aspects of the paper.

4. Broad empirical coverage
The experiments span multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple FM backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods. This breadth is valuable.

5. Good empirical gains in several settings
The improvements on Waterbirds and Metashift are substantial, and the component analysis broadly supports the intended role of CSA vs. LPA/RCB under different shifts.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Heavy dependence on non-interpretable pseudo-labelers
A central concern is that adaptation is driven by pseudo-labels obtained from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictors. In many settings, these predictors are already strong and sometimes stronger than the CBM. This raises a basic question: is CONDA adapting the CBM to the target domain, or is it distilling the target-domain behavior of a stronger black-box predictor into a concept bottleneck?

This does not invalidate the approach, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. The method may be better described as “post-hoc concept distillation under shift” rather than purely unsupervised adaptation of an interpretable model. The paper should discuss this more explicitly.

Relatedly, the fairness of comparisons is somewhat unclear:
- Are the direct LP/ZS baselines also allowed to adapt at test time?
- If not, then CONDA is being compared against static black-box baselines while itself using those black-box models to generate supervision.
This is not necessarily unfair, but it should be framed carefully.

2. Limited comparison to generic adaptation baselines on the same architecture
The paper compares mainly to unadapted CBMs and to non-interpretable ZS/LP predictors. What seems missing are stronger adaptation baselines that operate on the same CBM architecture or on the equivalent linear map W C phi(x):
- entropy minimization on the CBM logits,
- pseudo-label fine-tuning of the full linear map without preserving concept structure,
- adaptation of only W C jointly as a single linear layer,
- source-free adaptation methods such as TENT/MEMO/CAFA adapted to the CBM output or concept space.

Without these comparisons, it is hard to know whether the gains come from the concept-specific design or simply from doing pseudo-label-based online adaptation of a shallow classifier.

3. Theoretical framing is mostly taxonomy, not theory
Section 2 presents definitions of low-level shift, concept-level shift, completeness, and failure modes. This is useful as a conceptual taxonomy, but the paper occasionally suggests a stronger formal contribution than is actually delivered. There are no guarantees, bounds, or even propositions connecting the proposed objectives to improved target risk. For example:
- Why should minimizing the log ratio of intra/inter Mahalanobis distances recover a useful concept bank?
- Under what assumptions does CSA preserve semantics of concepts?
- When does RCB recover missing concepts rather than arbitrary discriminative directions?

I would encourage the authors to tone down the formal claims or strengthen them with at least some proposition-level analysis.

4. Interpretability claims are not fully substantiated
The paper claims that CONDA yields “concept-based interpretations better aligned with the test data.” The qualitative Waterbirds example is suggestive, but the evidence is limited.

Several concerns:
- Adapting concept vectors continuously may drift them away from their original semantic meaning.
- Residual concepts are learned from unlabeled target data with only weak regularization; they may become arbitrary discriminative directions rather than human-meaningful concepts.
- Automatic annotation of residual concepts is not sufficient evidence of interpretability.

The paper would be stronger with quantitative interpretability evaluations, e.g. concept coherence, stability, human agreement, sparsity/fidelity tradeoffs, or intervention-based usefulness. As written, the interpretability claims feel under-supported relative to the accuracy claims.

5. Some empirical results are mixed and deserve more discussion
Not all adaptation helps. For example, on CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 for some CBM variants, CONDA reduces AVG/WG relative to the unadapted model. Also, in the component analysis, using all components can underperform a subset. This is actually interesting, but the paper mostly emphasizes positive cases.

The method appears sensitive to shift type and CBM construction. More discussion is needed on:
- when CSA hurts,
- when RCB hurts,
- whether there is a reliable criterion for deciding which components to activate,
- whether online adaptation accumulates errors over batches.

6. Source statistics assumption in CSA may be restrictive
CSA assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source concept scores. This is lighter than storing source data, but still requires retaining per-class means and covariances. For large concept banks, covariance estimation and inversion may be unstable or expensive. The paper should clarify:
- whether full or diagonal covariances are used,
- how covariance regularization is handled,
- sensitivity to estimation quality,
- memory/computation overhead as m grows.

7. Methodological clarity issues
A few parts of the method are not fully clear:
- Are concept vectors renormalized after each gradient step?
- Is the FM feature extractor always frozen? It seems yes, but this should be stated consistently.
- In Eq. (12), cosine similarity regularization appears to penalize raw cosine, not absolute cosine. Does this encourage anti-correlated concepts rather than orthogonal/non-redundant ones?
- In Eq. (13), maximizing average similarity to top-k neighbors may encourage prototype-like directions, but why is this the right notion of concept coherence here?
- The notation around Eq. (5) and references to Eq. (3) later seem inconsistent.
- The Mahalanobis distance formula appears to have a parenthesis typo.

8. Evaluation protocol may blur adaptation and inference
The paper follows online TTA, adapting on each batch and predicting on the same batch. This is standard in some TTA work, but it can overestimate practical performance compared to predicting first and then adapting, especially when pseudo-labels are used on the same batch. The paper should be explicit about this and ideally report a stricter protocol as well.

Detailed comments and questions

1. Novelty relative to prior work
The residual branch resembles residual/incremental CBM ideas from recent work. The novelty here is mainly combining this with source-free adaptation and FM-based pseudo-labeling. That is still meaningful, but the paper should sharpen what is genuinely new versus assembled from existing ingredients.

2. On the definition of “concept-level shift”
The paper defines concept-level shift as one where concept-score distributions change but prediction distributions remain the same. This is a useful abstraction, but in practice on datasets like Waterbirds the target label distribution and spurious correlations may both change. The formalism may not cleanly match the benchmark construction. I would present this more as an idealized lens than a literal characterization.

3. Completeness definition
Definition 1 says a concept set is complete if there exists a classifier g such that prediction distributions are identical across source and target. This is unusual: completeness is usually tied to sufficiency for labels, not equality of prediction distributions across domains. As written, completeness depends jointly on the domains and shift family, not just on the concept set. That may be acceptable, but it should be acknowledged because it differs from standard usage.

4. Why should CSA preserve interpretability?
If concept vectors are updated freely in embedding space, they may cease to correspond to their original textual or semantic descriptions. The Frobenius penalty helps, but there is no explicit semantic anchoring. Did the authors measure concept drift, e.g. nearest text descriptions before/after adaptation or overlap in top activating examples?

5. Why not adapt only the residual branch?
Since modifying the main concept bank risks semantic drift, one alternative would be to keep the original concepts fixed and let only residual concepts absorb shift. An ablation comparing:
- only main-bank adaptation,
- only residual adaptation,
- both,
would help clarify the tradeoff between preserving semantics and improving accuracy.

6. Pseudo-label quality
The method’s success likely depends strongly on pseudo-label quality. I would like to see:
- pseudo-label accuracy on each dataset,
- confidence thresholding ablations,
- what happens when ZS and LP disagree,
- whether adaptation still helps when pseudo-labels are noisy.

7. Comparison to adapting direct LP
A particularly important baseline is: take the same FM features and adapt the direct linear probe using the same pseudo-labels and online protocol. If that adapted LP still outperforms CONDA by a large margin, then the contribution is mainly preserving some interpretability while sacrificing little accuracy. If CONDA matches it, that is stronger. But this comparison should be explicit.

8. Statistical significance and variance
Some reported gains are large and convincing, but others are small. It would help to report significance tests or at least clearer discussion of which improvements are robust across seeds.

9. Interpretability evaluation on residual concepts
The claim that residual concepts correspond to “feathers, wings, beak” is plausible, but qualitative examples can be cherry-picked. A more systematic evaluation would strengthen the paper:
- top-k image retrieval for residual concepts,
- concept purity judged by humans,
- overlap with known attributes where available,
- comparison to random directions or PCA directions.

10. Practicality
The paper mentions complexity in the appendix, but the main text should summarize runtime overhead. Since adaptation occurs online per batch with multiple gradient steps and covariance-based distances, deployment cost matters.

Minor issues

- There are several notation and formatting inconsistencies, likely due to manuscript conversion, but they should be cleaned up.
- Eq. numbering references appear inconsistent in a few places.
- The paper sometimes says “prediction distributions” when it seems to mean conditional label mappings or decision consistency.
- “Coherancy” should be “coherence” or “coherency” consistently.
- AVG and WG are described as per-class metrics, but for Waterbirds and similar datasets “worst-group accuracy” usually refers to subgroup accuracy, not per-class minimum. Please clarify exactly how groups are defined on each dataset.

Suggestions for improvement

1. Add stronger baselines
At minimum:
- pseudo-label adaptation of direct LP on FM features,
- entropy-minimization or pseudo-label adaptation of the CBM logits,
- joint adaptation of the equivalent linear map W C without concept-specific decomposition,
- a source-free adaptation baseline such as TENT/CAFA/MEMO adapted to the CBM setting.

2. Clarify the role of pseudo-labelers
Be explicit that the method leverages stronger black-box predictors for supervision at test time. Discuss whether this is acceptable in the intended deployment setting and what happens if only the CBM itself is available.

3. Strengthen interpretability evaluation
Include quantitative measures of concept coherence/stability and semantic drift, especially for adapted main concepts and residual concepts.

4. Improve analysis of when each component helps
A simple gating heuristic or diagnostic for selecting CSA vs. LPA vs. RCB would make the method more practical and would align with the paper’s own finding that not all components help on all shifts.

5. Tighten the theoretical claims
Either provide a modest proposition-level justification for CSA/RCB or present Section 2 more clearly as a conceptual taxonomy rather than a formal theory.

6. Clarify evaluation protocol
Report whether adaptation is performed before or after prediction on each batch, and ideally include a stricter protocol.

Recommendation

Weak Accept to Borderline

I like the problem, the empirical motivation, and the modular adaptation idea. The paper could have meaningful impact for interpretable deployment of FM-based systems. However, I have nontrivial reservations about the reliance on black-box pseudo-labelers, the lack of stronger adaptation baselines, and the limited evidence for interpretability preservation after adaptation. If these issues are addressed, the work would be substantially stronger.

Confidence

3/5

I am reasonably confident in my assessment of the paper’s strengths and weaknesses, though some concerns depend on appendix details and missing baseline specifics that may be clarified in a fuller version.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. The authors argue that although FM-based CBMs can be interpretable and competitive in-distribution, they often degrade substantially under low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts. They identify three failure modes—non-robust concept bottlenecks, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers, and incomplete concept sets—and propose CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: concept-score alignment (CSA) to adapt concept vectors via class-conditional Gaussian statistics and Mahalanobis distances, linear probing adaptation (LPA) to adapt the concept-to-label layer with pseudo-labels, and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) to add new concepts for missing target-domain semantics. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with multiple CBM construction methods show substantial target-domain gains in many settings, sometimes bringing CBM performance close to non-interpretable baselines while also yielding qualitatively adapted concept explanations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines built on foundation models.
Clear decomposition of failure modes under distribution shift, which provides an intuitive motivation for the three components of the method.
Method is modular and practically relevant: adapts concept bank, classifier, and residual concepts without source data or target labels.
Empirical evaluation is broad in terms of datasets, shift types, FM backbones, and CBM construction methods.
Results show strong improvements in many challenging settings, especially under concept-level shifts where unadapted CBMs degrade sharply.
Includes component-wise analysis showing that different adaptation stages matter for different shift types, which supports the design rationale.
Interpretability analysis is a useful addition and suggests that adaptation changes concept reliance in human-plausible ways.
The paper is generally well written and technically organized, with explicit objectives and algorithmic details.
weaknesses: The theoretical formalization of shift types and concept completeness is mostly descriptive and does not lead to formal guarantees for the proposed adaptation procedure.
The method relies heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictions; if these are poor or biased, adaptation may reinforce errors, and this dependency is not deeply analyzed.

CSA assumes access to source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics in concept space; this is weaker than source-data access but still requires storing privileged source summaries that may be nontrivial in some settings.
The Gaussian/Mahalanobis modeling assumption for concept scores may be crude, especially for multimodal or highly non-Gaussian concept distributions.
Some results indicate adaptation can hurt performance relative to the unadapted CBM (e.g., certain CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 configurations), suggesting instability or mismatch between components.

Comparisons are mainly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines rather than stronger generic TTA baselines adapted to the same CBM setting, limiting clarity on how much gain comes from standard adaptation machinery versus the concept-specific design.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative; there is limited quantitative evaluation of concept quality, faithfulness, or human usefulness after adaptation.
The residual branch improves expressiveness but may dilute the original bottleneck interpretability, especially if residual concepts are only weakly semantically grounded.
soundness_issues: The central adaptation objectives are plausible, but the paper does not provide strong justification that minimizing the proposed Mahalanobis ratio in CSA actually aligns target concept distributions in a way that preserves class semantics under pseudo-label noise.
Definition 1 of concept completeness is broad and somewhat idealized; it is not operationalized in a measurable way, yet motivates the residual concept mechanism.

The pseudo-labeling strategy selects the more confident prediction between zero-shot and linear probing, but confidence calibration across these predictors may not be comparable; this heuristic may be brittle.
Online adaptation on test batches can be order-sensitive and susceptible to error accumulation, but robustness to batch order or stream composition is not discussed in the main text.

The residual concept objective includes coherence and similarity regularization, but there is limited evidence that these terms reliably produce semantically meaningful and non-redundant concepts rather than merely improving accuracy.

Because the method uses target unlabeled data for adaptation and evaluates on the same stream, care is needed to distinguish online adaptation gains from broader generalization; the setup follows TTA conventions but still inherits their evaluation caveats.
